stimulus.text:
American losses in the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, December 7, 1941.

| Americans killed | 2,403 |
| Americans wounded | 1,178 |
| Battleships sunk or damaged | 8 |
| Aircraft destroyed | 188 |
| Japanese aircraft lost | 29 |
stimulus.source_note: Figures from the Department of Defense 50th Anniversary of World War II Commemorative Committee summary of the attack, corroborated by the 5 Steps day-item record (2,403 killed, 1,178 wounded). All eight battleships present were damaged, four sunk; six returned to service during the war.

source: original; stimulus drawn from book-grounded figures and paraphrases (see source_note)
stem: The losses in the table came from the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. What did the attack lead most directly to?

options.text: Japan surrendered to the United States
options.misconception: Japan did not surrender until 1945, after two atomic bombs and years of war.

options.text: The United States joined the League of Nations
options.misconception: The United States never joined the League of Nations; the Senate rejected membership in 1919.

options.text: The United States declared war on Japan
Germany declared war on the Soviet Union
options.misconception: Germany had already invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941; it declared war on the United States, not the Soviet Union.

rationales.A: Japan fought on for nearly four more years; surrender came in 1945, not 1941.
rationales.B: The United States never joined the League; the Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles in 1919.
rationales.C: Congress declared war on Japan on December 8, 1941, the day after the attack.
rationales.D: Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, months before Pearl Harbor.
rationales.general:
1. The table shows a surprise attack that killed more than 2,400 Americans and crippled the Pacific Fleet.
2. Before the attack, most Americans wanted to stay out of the war.
3. Background from the books: the attack ended that debate overnight, and Congress declared war on Japan the next day.
4. The other choices place later events in 1941 or describe things that never happened.
Remember: a surprise attack on American forces usually ends debate about entering a war.
